newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis jittery as Islamist deadline approaches.
newsitem.headline: Israelis jittery as Islamist deadline approaches.

text.p: An Islamic militant ultimatum coupled with the threat of more suicide attacks gave Israelis the jitters on Sunday.
Police Chief Assaf Hefetz warned Israelis still in mourning for the 13 people killed by two suicide bombers in Jerusalem last week that militants could strike again.
Israel Radio said police received hundreds of calls from citizens reporting suspicious objects.

Police were taking all precautions ahead of a demand that Israel free all Palestinian prisoners by 9 p.m. (1800 GMT) on Sunday. A leaflet claiming the attack on Wednesday in the name of the Islamic militant Hamas group made the demand.
Israeli police spokeswoman Linda Menuhin said on Sunday: "I can tell you we are taking every threat seriously."
All the same, some Israeli and Palestinian officials voiced doubts about the leaflet's authenticity.
Israel announced no plans to free anyone. The leaflet did not spell out what would happen if Israel refused.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told his cabinet that Israel would not honour peace deals it signed with Yasser Arafat unless the Palestinian leader cracked down on militants.

"If Arafat honours his commitments in the agreement, chiefly to fight terrorism, the agreement will survive. If he doesn't, we will not keep up our part of the bargain unequivocally," an official statement quoted Netanyahu as saying.
Thousands of policemen guarded shopping malls, bus stations and other places where crowds gather in Israel's main cities and stopped cars for inspection along key roads.

Troops overnight arrested another 37 Palestinians in the West Bank suspected of involvement in Islamic militant groups, bringing to 116 the number arrested since the bombing in the main Jewish street market.
Hefetz, asked if Israel had specific information about more attacks, told army radio: "It's more than just an estimate. We have a series of...details that point to this possibility."
He said after four days of investigation, officials were still uncertain who carried out the attack.
The suicide bombing revived haunting memories of a bombing spree last year in which Islamic miliants struck four times in nine days, killing 57 people.

Para-military border policeman armed with automatic rifles patrolled a stretch of Jerusalem road from the bombing site at the Mahane Yehuda market to the city's central station where morning commuters rushed to catch their buses.
"I'm not afraid. There's a God in heaven...It's all in God's hands," said Jerusalem-born Moshe Levy, 74, boarding a bus for a day of recreation in Tel Aviv.
Two of the four bombs last year exploded on Jerusalem buses.
"Coming to Israel you make a decision to put yourself in a place where things happen," said tourist Miriam Ratowitz, 22, of Chicago, who was waiting for a bus with American friends.
Police later held up traffic for nearly an hour near the station while sappers exploded a duffel bag left behind by a traveller and suspected of containing a bomb.

Israel suspended already dormant peace talks with the Palestinians as a result of the bombing and sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, barring tens of thousands of Palestinians from reaching their jobs in the Jewish state.

Palestinians accused Israel of imposing collective punishment on Palestinians and expressed hope U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross, due later this week on another mediation mission, could put peacemaking back on track.

"The closure is a kind of a massive, collective punishment...It is a closure that will help, once again, the extremist policies and tendencies in the region," said Yasser Abed Rabbo, the Palestinian information minister.
Top Israeli security officials met their Palestinian counterparts overnight to discuss the investigation into Wednesday's bombing, security sources said.
But Jibril al-Rajoub, the head of the Palestinian preventive security in the West Bank, said the meetings did not constitute a renewal of security cooperation.
